doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Cafe Wha? sessions and being hired by Mingus
summary: At Greenwich Village jam sessions, Mingus needed alto and trumpet players, heard McPherson and Hillyer, and hired them alongside the departing Eric Dolphy.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Peter Stookey, right. No, it’s not, it’s Paul Stookey.

Well I knew him as Noel. Oh, okay. All right. Now he was just a folk singer singing, playing his guitar, and then we had this jam session in the afternoon, and Bill Cosby or people like that or even Bob Dylan would be at some coffee house across the street, and everybody was just like struggling nonentities basically, really. And so in the afternoon we’d have these sessions. And Mingus came by one afternoon because he was in need of an alto player and a trumpet player. And we were recommended by Yusef, who worked with Mingus sometimes, and Eric Dolphy and a guy named Ted Curson, trumpet player, both respectively were going to quit Mingus and get their own groups. And so Mingus needed a saxophone player in there. And he was really mad at Eric and both of those guys. But anyway he came to the session in the afternoon and heard us and he hired us. He told us, “Well come to the club tonight and bring your horns and we’ll see what happens.” And Eric Dolphy was still there, because they had two weeks notice. So for about two weeks there were two altos and two trumpets in Mingus’ band. And Mingus, every night, tried to get Eric not to quit. Because Eric really played Mingus’ music well. And he had been working with Mingus a long time. And Mingus’ music was extremely difficult. It takes a long time to teach people these songs and then here Eric is going to quit. But anyway, the memorable thing that happened is Lonnie and I were in this club, owned by a gangster, definitely that scene. And we were in the club and it was at the end of the evening. And these people owed Mingus about two thousand dollars. That was the first time Lonnie and I had been in the company of Mingus like this. And so Mingus — the money was not there — and Mingus at this time weighed about three hundred pounds, probably 40 years old or so. He just tore the piano up. It was a Steinway grand, probably seven feet. He went inside the piano and took his fingers and plucked the strings, all that tension. You know piano wires hold locomotives.
